name: Liam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am the senior drill operator at Granite Reach mine, and I set the pattern before the crew starts a new face. I have a two-year technical diploma, but the younger operators ask me about sound and vibration more than paperwork. My wife Mara works at a clinic, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I have never used an AI tool; a drill is enough technology for one man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that if AI only tidies a few forms, we should get on with drilling. The mine has bought clever software before and the rock did not care. I would still check every hole position myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my wage to hold. We have a good savings buffer, Mara’s clinic pay, and other mines within driving distance. I worry more about a costly drill repair than about routine forms moving to a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the drill patterns and checking the holes before the first blast. I would let the clerk handle the new forms while I compare the printed plan with the face. In the first year I would keep our mortgage payments and family budget as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I know the work and the bills are covered, although a bad bit can ruin a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would you catch on the printed plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hole too close to a cracked edge is trouble. I would walk the line with the junior operator before marking it. A printed drill plan cannot feel the ground under a boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the form tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to for the job. I am not against a machine doing clerical work; I just do not want another screen in the drill cab. The clerk is quicker at that part.

say: I would let **software** tidy forms while the crew keeps drilling and checking the face.
I would still check **hole positions** myself before a blast.
think: My **wage** looks steady, supported by savings, my wife’s income and nearby mines.
A **drill repair** worries me more than forms moving onto a screen.
do: **Keep** setting Granite Reach drill patterns and checking marked holes.
**Compare** each printed plan with the actual face before drilling.
S0.quote: A printed drill plan cannot feel the ground under a boot.
fieldNote: His **senior skill** rests on ground feel and careful checks rather than digital tools.
He has **strong savings** and another household earner, so little AI change feels manageable.
He leaves new forms to the **clerk** while retaining responsibility for hole safety.

steps.text: Keep setting drill patterns and checking holes before blasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software can make a schedule, but the drill crew must sign off on the holes. Buying and dispatch might change first. I would tell management that an old hand should check every new plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work still needs a person while robots spread slowly, so my pay looks fairly secure. I do worry that the mine will remove a junior operator to save wages. That would put more checking on me and less learning in the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down our current checking time before the new schedule starts. I would ask the foreman for a weekly walk of the drill line with the junior operator. If the mine cut that time, I would bring the figures to a crew meeting rather than learn a new screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can keep earning, but a rushed crew is an accident waiting to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the crew meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show that the walk takes twenty minutes and catches holes beside weak rock. I would ask the foreman to put that time back on the schedule. Losing twenty minutes of drill-line checks can cost a whole shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek another mine if junior posts went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first see whether the crew could fix the schedule. There are plenty of mines nearby, but I would not leave my team over one bad plan. I might look if the checking time stayed gone.

say: I would insist a **drill operator** sign off on hole plans made by software.
I would protect **checking time** for a junior operator to learn the face.
think: My **own pay** looks fairly secure while robots enter hands-on work slowly.
Fewer **junior posts** could leave the crew rushed and less skilled.
do: **Record** current drill-line checking time before a new schedule starts.
**Ask** the foreman to keep a weekly walk with the junior operator.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed checks, though his income appears safe.
S1.quote: Losing twenty minutes of drill-line checks can cost a whole shift.
fieldNote: He sees **planning and buying** changing before drilling itself.
His defence of **apprenticeship time** fits a senior operator who teaches by walking the face.
He would try a **crew meeting** before considering a move to another mine.

steps.text: Keep checking drill line with junior operator each week
Bring lost checking time to drill crew meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full thinking AI by 2028 changes the plans first, not the drill steel. Capable robots arrive around 2031 in this picture, and the mine might then buy them. I would ask management for a written timetable and a fair apprenticeship plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose the senior drill wage if capable robots replace our crew around 2031. I would be forty-eight then, with two children still depending on us and a mortgage to pay. Savings and Mara’s clinic wage help, but I cannot know whether her work stays steady either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put our planned family holiday on hold and ask the lender what six months on one income would mean. I would keep drilling after 2028, checking any AI plan against the rock myself. I would ask the foreman about paid mechanical training, and take a place only if it led to a real job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would be awake counting mortgage payments, even with money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the holiday would you cancel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flights and the rented cabin would wait. I would tell the children why without making them carry my fear. We could still visit their grandparents by car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the foreman offers training without a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would thank him and keep my wage for now. A mechanical certificate is no use if every mine is cutting drill crews. I would ask other mines what mechanics they actually need.

say: I would explain **2028** changes plans before capable robot drills might arrive around 2031.
I would ask management for a **written timetable** and a fair apprenticeship route.
think: My **senior wage** could go around 2031 if the mine buys capable robots.
Our **savings** help, but children, mortgage and uncertainty about my wife’s hours keep me awake.
do: **Delay** booking flights and cabin for the family holiday.
**Ask** the lender about six months on one income.
**Keep** drilling after 2028 while checking AI plans against the face.
feel: **Alarmed** by a possible loss of his main wage and mortgage pressure.
S2.quote: A mechanical certificate is no use if every mine is cutting drill crews.
fieldNote: He correctly separates **2028 thinking AI** from capable robots around 2031.
He expects his own **wage** may go and describes lost sleep despite substantial savings.
He will take mechanical training only if it is **paid** and linked to a real job.

steps.text: Delay booking family holiday flights and rented cabin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years before thinking AI and about eight before capable robots is time to prepare properly. The mine should keep apprenticeships running and tell families when posts might change. I would ask for an honest equipment schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be forty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2031 and around fifty-one when capable robots appear in 2034. I might have enough time to finish a mechanical trade, if there are jobs for it. My savings let me pay for some classes, but I would still want a position to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in a part-time mechanical certificate next autumn if a nearby mine posted technician openings. I would take the first module while keeping my drill wage, and put an extra amount toward the mortgage each month after checking penalties. I would also keep teaching the junior operator on the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a route. Eight years is long enough to earn a second certificate without asking my family to live on hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the technical college and ask what work the graduates actually get. Then I would check the nearby mine postings myself. I will not enrol because a brochure has a nice photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no technician openings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the drill wage and wait rather than pay for the course. I could look again the following year. The mortgage does not care how eager I am to retrain.

say: I would use the **eight-year warning** to seek a real mechanical route before capable robots around 2034.
I would keep **apprenticeships** running while current drill crews still work.
think: At about **fifty-one** when robots become capable, I may have time for a second trade.
I would need **real technician openings** before paying for training.
do: **Enrol** in a part-time mechanical certificate if nearby mines post technician work.
**Pay** extra toward the mortgage monthly after checking loan penalties.
**Keep** teaching the junior drill operator while earning my wage.
feel: **Anxious**, with a possible route into another trade.
S3.quote: The mortgage does not care how eager I am to retrain.
fieldNote: Age is **forty-eight** in 2031 and about fifty-one when capable robots arrive in 2034.
He will **self-fund** classes only after seeing actual technician openings.
Teaching the junior operator remains part of his **work identity**.

steps.text: Enrol in part-time mechanical certificate if local technician openings appear
Pay extra toward mortgage monthly after checking penalties
Keep teaching junior drill operator on current shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the mine has ten years before thinking AI and about thirteen before capable robots can drill. That is enough time for proper apprenticeships and honest family planning. I would ask management to set out the equipment plan in plain words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be fifty-three in 2036 and around fifty-six when capable robots arrive in 2039. If the mortgage shrinks as planned, we might be able to retire then, but I need the pension statement first. I would rather keep drilling well than chase a tool I do not trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the drill crew and put the junior operator through the usual hands-on checks. At home I would request pension and mortgage statements this year and review them with Mara. I would keep the present payments until we knew whether an earlier retirement was affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the younger men and women who would still have long loans, though my own income feels fairly secure. A long warning gives my family time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the figures have to come first. My wife Mara and I would decide together when the mortgage and pension statements arrive. I would not promise the children a date I cannot afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the junior operator learn before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to hear a bit dragging and how to see a crack before the plan marks it. I would make time each shift for junior drill operators to learn cracks and dragging bits. I would make time for that every shift.

say: I would ask the mine for a **plain equipment plan** during the long warning.
I would protect **hands-on apprenticeship** time while people still run drills.
think: At about **fifty-six** when robots become capable, retirement might be affordable if mortgage and pension figures allow.
I would rather keep **drilling well** than chase unfamiliar software.
do: **Keep** leading the drill crew and teaching physical checks each shift.
**Request** pension and mortgage statements this year and review them with Mara.
feel: **Uneasy** for younger operators, steadier about his own income.
S4.quote: I would make time each shift for junior drill operators to learn cracks and dragging bits.
fieldNote: His **retirement possibility** depends on mortgage and pension figures, not an assumed date.
He preserves **hands-on teaching** and avoids AI tools, consistent with his habits.
The long runway shifts most of his concern toward **younger operators**.

steps.text: Keep leading drill crew and teaching physical checks each shift
Request pension and mortgage statements before setting retirement date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot drills could follow around 2031, while our children and mortgage still depend on my wage. A written mine timetable and paid mechanical training tied to real posts would help. I would also want time to keep teaching the junior crew.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who takes responsibility for a bad hole when the plan comes from software. I have signed my name to drill patterns for years. I would not put my name on a plan nobody could explain.

headlineQuote: I would not put my name on a plan nobody could explain.
portrait: Liam Hansen is a **43-year-old** senior drill operator at Granite Reach mine, with two children, a mortgage and substantial savings.
His **technical diploma** and years teaching junior operators make him confident in physical checks, while he avoids AI tools.
Mild change leaves his **income secure**; faster robot availability threatens his wage and brings mortgage worries despite savings.
With more warning he considers a **mechanical certificate** only if real jobs appear, and weighs retirement against actual pension figures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable robot drills could follow around 2031 while his household depends on his wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **written timetable** and paid mechanical training linked to real posts would help him plan for possible lost drill work.
